title: Achilles: the heel and invulnerability
subtitle: Glory and the weak point
subject: mythologie
description: Achilles, the hero of the Iliad, looks unbeatable. One heel, one arrow, and the myth invents the universal metaphor for a fatal weak point.

hero.hook: The greatest warrior at Troy. Skin almost impossible to pierce. And one heel that changed the meaning of the word “weakness.”

blocks.text: **Achilles** is the central hero of the **Iliad**, Homer's poem about the Trojan War. Son of the nymph **Thetis** and the mortal **Peleus**, he is the perfect warrior: fast, fierce, obsessed with [[Kleos]], the glory that outlives death.
His story mixes near-divine power with certain death. One detail of the body, the heel, became the universal symbol of the flaw hidden inside strength.

A prophecy says that Achilles will be stronger than his father. **Zeus** and **Poseidon** therefore give up Thetis and marry her to Peleus. To protect the child, Thetis dips him in the **Styx**, the river of the underworld whose water is said to make skin impossible to pierce.

blocks.caption: Thetis dips Achilles in the Styx, holding him by the heel

blocks.text: The magical version of the invulnerability shows up late, in the poet [[Statius]] (1st century AD). In Homer, no spell protects Achilles: he is simply the best fighter, and still mortal.
She holds him by the **heel**. That patch of skin stays dry, and so stays vulnerable. A technical detail becomes the heart of the myth.

Outside Troy, Achilles withdraws from the fighting after an insult from **Agamemnon**, the leader of the Greeks, who takes his captive [[Briseis]] from him. Without him the Achaean army collapses. What brings him back to the front is the death of **Patroclus**, his dearest companion.

blocks.caption: Achilles against Hector, the decisive duel below the walls of Troy

blocks.text: He puts on armor forged by [[Hephaestus]], the blacksmith god, and launches an [[aristeia]], a run of superhuman feats in battle. He kills **Hector**, prince of Troy, then drags his body behind his chariot. That [[hubris]], that excess of pride, is shocking. Only a night visit from old King **Priam** brings Achilles back to his humanity: he finally gives up the body for burial.
Achilles was offered a choice: a long life nobody would remember, or a short life famous forever. He chose glory. That choice defines Greek tragic heroism.

Below the walls of Troy, **Paris**, an archer prince nobody admired for his courage, lets an arrow fly. Guided by **Apollo**, it strikes Achilles in the heel. The greatest warrior falls to the least brave of the fighters.

blocks.caption: The death of Achilles: the arrow of Paris finds the heel

blocks.text: His ashes are mixed with those of Patroclus. Even dead, Achilles is still worth fighting over: the Greeks quarrel about his weapons. The age of heroes begins to close.

The phrase “**Achilles' heel**” still names the flaw in a system that looks solid. Anatomy keeps the same story: the [[Achilles' heel]] gave its name to the thick tendon above the heel bone. In politics, in computing, in strategy, the idea stays the same: nothing is stronger than its weakest link.
Beyond the metaphor, Achilles carries the Greek dilemma: live long in the shade, or burn briefly and stay immortal in the stories. By choosing battle, he won immortality in literature.
Almost impossible to wound thanks to the Styx, Achilles dies at Troy from an arrow in the heel. The myth leaves us the [[Achilles' heel]] and the universal image of one fatal weakness.
